processing: A green tea made from tender, downy shoots. Little is documented about the exact steps; the fixing and drying are presumably those of other fine Shaanxi greens.
harvest_season: Spring is usual for a fine green of this kind; the local leaf is valued for thick, downy young shoots.
appearance_dry: Downy green leaf, with white hair on the tender shoots.
appearance_liquor: Likely a clear pale green, as is typical of southern Shaanxi greens.
appearance_wet: Tender, thick shoots, as the local leaf is described.
taste_profile: Few tasting notes are recorded for this tea; expect the fresh, softly sweet character typical of Qinba mountain greens.

brewing.notes: These are general settings for a downy green. Some haze from the down is normal.

vintage_note: As is usual for its class, it should be bought as the current year's spring tea and drunk within about a year. No aged form exists to look for.
description:
Qinba Wuhao is a green tea from Zhenba county in southern Shaanxi, on the divide between the Han and Jialing rivers. The name means roughly Qinba mist and down: Qinba for the place, mist for the climate, and down for the white hair on the young leaf.

The gardens sit among steep, foggy hills with deep soil, little sun and damp air. Most bushes are the Ziyang Zhuye cultivar, and the shoots are thick and hairy. Beyond that, little is documented about how the leaf is worked.

In the cup, treat it as you would other Qinba greens: cool water, a light dose and short attention. Specific tasting notes for this tea are scarce, so trust your own cup over a seller's list.

It counts among the teas within the Hanzhong Xianhao family. Claims about selenium and long lists of health benefits are common on packaging and are no guide to quality.
history:
Local legend calls the older tea Kouhan Cha, mouth-held tea: pickers were said to hold each bud in the mouth before it was dried, and Liu Bang is said to have drunk it while King of Hanzhong. These stories are legends, not documented history.

The modern tea dates to 1984, when it was developed by a company that grew out of the Zhenba county forestry and tea station. That December, Professor Chen Chuan of the Anhui Agricultural College visited Zhenba and gave it its present name.
